reason: The verifier’s correction is right and I confirmed it at the page. The Wikisource transcription of The Single Hound prints the poem as “XXXVIII. / A LITTLE madness in the Spring / Is wholesome even for the King, / But God be with the Clown, / Who ponders this tremendous scene— / This whole experiment of green, / As if it were his own!”, and its header gives “Boston: Little, Brown and company, page 40”. So the number XXXVIII holds, the page holds, and the 1914 book’s house styling holds exactly as the note claims: lower-case “madness” and “experiment of green” where the manuscript-based modern texts print capitals, a comma after “Clown” where they print a dash, and the dash kept after “scene”. “A LITTLE” is the book’s display capital on the opening words, so rendering it “A little” is normalisation of type, not a change of wording. The Part II claim is dead as the note says: the page navigation runs straight from ‘“Morning” means “Milking” to the Farmer’ to “I can’t tell you, but you feel it” with no part heading between, and the volume’s numbering runs through. Attribution right, no speaker, no translator, complete poem so no locator risk, in scope (posthumous 1914, written c. 1875), publishable, and on theme. Source leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote, 103 characters; tag Poetry correct. Two things for the editor, neither a refutation. One, the evidence calls the scan “the 1914 Little, Brown edition”; the djvu’s title page reads “BOSTON / LITTLE, BROWN, AND COMPANY / 1915” and its copyright page “Copyright, 1914, By Martha Dickinson Bianchi”, so what was read is the 1915 impression from the 1914 plates. The card’s date of 1914 is right for the edition and the pagination is the same, but the evidence should say which printing it saw. Two, shipped.js puts Dickinson at two of three for the year, from months 1 and 2, so this is her last line and nothing further can be spent on her; she appears once in April, and the quotation itself is not shipped and has nothing near it.
